title: Σὺς καὶ κύων ⟨ἀλλήλαις λοιδορούμεναι⟩
titleEn: The Sow and the Dog Reviling One Another
part: The Sow and the Dog Reviling One Another (Chambry 329 · Perry 222)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 329 (= Perry 222). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A sow and a dog were reviling one another.
sentences.n: Both animals are female here — σῦς a sow, κύων a she-dog — which is why ἀλλήλαις is feminine, and the quarrel turns on what each of them is fit for. διαλοιδορέομαι has δια- of exchange: abuse passing back and forth.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἡ μὲν σῦς ὤμνυε κατὰ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης ἦ μὴν τοῖς ὀδοῦσιν ἀναρρήξειν τὴν κύνα.
sentences.tr: Kai hē men sys ōmnye kata tēs Aphroditēs ē mēn tois odousin anarrēxein tēn kyna.
sentences.l: And the sow swore by Aphrodite that she would assuredly tear the dog open with her teeth.
sentences.n: ὄμνυμι κατά with the genitive is the regular way of swearing by a god: the κατά is 'down upon', from the hand laid on the victims or the altar sworn over. ἦ μήν is the solemn formula that introduces what is sworn, and the future infinitive ἀναρρήξειν holds it.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ κύων πρὸς ταῦτα εἰρωνικῶς εἶπε· « Καλῶς κατὰ τῆς Ἀφροδίτης ἡμῖν ὀμνύεις· δηλοῖς γὰρ ὑπ’ αὐτῆς ὅτι μάλιστα φιλεῖσθαι, ἣ τὸν τῶν σῶν ἀκαθάρτων σαρκῶν γευόμενον οὐδ’ ὅλως εἰς ἱερὸν προσίεται. »
sentences.tr: Hē de kyōn pros tauta eirōnikōs eipe· « Kalōs kata tēs Aphroditēs hēmin omnyeis· dēlois gar hyp’ autēs hoti malista phileisthai, hē ton tōn sōn akathartōn sarkōn geuomenon oud’ holōs eis hieron prosietai. »
sentences.l: And the dog said to this mockingly: « Finely do you swear to us by Aphrodite; for you make it plain that you are loved by her as much as ever can be — she who does not admit into her temple at all the one who tastes of your unclean flesh. »
sentences.i: And the dog said to this, with heavy irony: « How well you swear to us by Aphrodite! You make it perfectly plain how dearly she loves you — she who will not let anyone who tastes your unclean flesh into her temple at all. »
sentences.n: ὅτι μάλιστα is the idiom of ὅτι with a superlative, 'as much as ever can be', not the conjunction 'that'; the infinitive φιλεῖσθαι depends on δηλοῖς. καλῶς at the head is bitter. γευόμενον is a present participle, so the man is shut out for eating pork at all, not for one past meal. The gibe rests on cult usage: swine were no offering to Aphrodite, and the dog goes further, saying that whoever so much as tastes pork is shut out of her precinct altogether.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἡ σῦς· « Διὰ τοῦτο μὲν οὖν μᾶλλον δήλη ἐστὶν ἡ θεὸς στέργουσά με· τὸν γὰρ κτείναντα ἢ ἄλλως λυμαινόμενον παντάπασιν ἀποστρέφεται· σὺ μέντοι κακῶς ὄζεις καὶ ζῶσα καὶ τεθνηκυῖα. »
sentences.tr: Kai hē sys· « Dia touto men oun mallon dēlē estin hē theos stergousa me· ton gar kteinanta ē allōs lymainomenon pantapasin apostrephetai· sy mentoi kakōs ozeis kai zōsa kai tethnēkuia. »
sentences.l: And the sow: « For this very reason, rather, the goddess is the more plainly fond of me; for she turns utterly away from the one who kills me or otherwise does me violence. You, though, smell foul both alive and dead. »
sentences.i: And the sow: « That is all the more reason to say the goddess is fond of me: she turns her back completely on anyone who kills me or does me any other harm. You, though, stink both alive and dead. »
sentences.n: The verb of speaking is simply left out after Καὶ ἡ σῦς, as often in these exchanges. δήλη ἐστὶ στέργουσα is the personal construction Greek prefers — 'she is plain, being fond of me' where English says 'it is plain that she is fond of me' — with a supplementary participle attached to the subject. μὲν οὖν takes up the other speaker's point and turns it round: 'nay rather'. τεθνηκυῖα is the perfect participle of θνῄσκω, the ordinary word for 'dead'.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ φρόνιμοι τῶν ῥητόρων τὰ ὑπὸ τῶν ἐχθρῶν ὀνείδη εὐμεθόδως εἰς ἔπαινον μετασχηματίζουσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti hoi phronimoi tōn rhētorōn ta hypo tōn echthrōn oneidē eumethodōs eis epainon metaschēmatizousin.
sentences.l: The fable shows that the shrewd among orators skilfully turn the reproaches that come from their enemies into praise.
sentences.n: εὐμεθόδως is 'by good method', the practised turn of a trained speaker. μετασχηματίζω is to change a thing's shape into another shape — here the insult re-figured as a compliment, which is precisely what the sow has just done.
